column6: Wash your panels the smart way
column8:
☀️ Solar tip #001 · For every home

Wash your panels the smart way

Rinse with plain water early in the morning or at sunset. Never splash cold water on hot glass at midday, and skip soap and hard brushes.

Lebanese dust and pollen settle fast, especially after a dry spell or a sandstorm. A gentle rinse every few weeks keeps output up. A soft mop with a long handle is enough; abrasive pads scratch the anti-reflective coating.

column6: Design Voc for the coldest morning
column8:
☀️ Solar tip #002 · For the technical crowd

Design Voc for the coldest morning

Voc rises as cells get colder. Correct string Voc to the site's minimum temperature and stay under the inverter's max DC input.

Use the module's Voc temperature coefficient (typically around −0.25 to −0.3 %/°C). Mountain sites in Lebanon can see sub-zero winter mornings, which pushes Voc well above STC.

column6: Run heavy loads between 10:00 and 15:00

☀️ Solar tip #003 · For every home

Run heavy loads between 10:00 and 15:00

Washing machine, water pump, electric heater, ironing: schedule them while the sun is high and your panels are at their peak.

Every kWh you use straight from the panels is a kWh your battery doesn't have to store and your generator doesn't have to make. Timers and smart plugs make this automatic.

column6: Check Vmp at hot cell temperature
column8:
☀️ Solar tip #004 · For the technical crowd

Check Vmp at hot cell temperature

At a summer cell temperature of around 70°C, the string Vmp must still sit inside the inverter's MPPT window.

Too few modules per string and the hot-day voltage drops below the tracker's minimum, so the inverter loses the MPP exactly when irradiance is highest.

column6: Don't empty your battery every night
column8:
☀️ Solar tip #005 · For every home

Don't empty your battery every night

Keep a reserve of about 20% in a lithium battery. Deep daily discharges shorten its life.

Most hybrid inverters let you set a minimum state of charge. Ask your installer to set a sensible cut-off so the battery always has a buffer for the morning and for cloudy days.

One MPPT, one orientation, one module

Don't mix module models, tilts or azimuths on the same MPPT input. Mismatch costs yield.

Use separate MPPT inputs for east and west arrays, or for strings with different module counts.

column6: One shadow can cost a whole string
column8:
☀️ Solar tip #007 · For every home

One shadow can cost a whole string

A water tank, antenna or satellite dish shading a single panel can pull down the output of every panel wired with it.

Panels in a string behave like a chain: the weakest link sets the pace. Before installing, walk the roof at 9:00, 12:00 and 15:00 and note every shadow. Move small obstacles if you can.

column6: Keep DC voltage drop under about 1.5%

☀️ Solar tip #008 · For the technical crowd

Keep DC voltage drop under about 1.5%

Size DC cables for voltage drop, not just ampacity. UV-rated solar cable, 4 or 6 mm² for most residential strings.

Long roof-to-basement runs are common in Lebanese buildings. Calculate the drop for the full loop length (go and return).

column6: Never mix MC4 brands
column8:
☀️ Solar tip #010 · For the technical crowd

Never mix MC4 brands

Mated connectors from different manufacturers are a classic cause of hot joints and fires. Same brand, proper crimp tool.

Cross-mated connectors void warranties and can fail open-circuit or overheat. Crimp, don't solder, and pull-test every joint.

column6: Hot panels make less power
column8:
☀️ Solar tip #011 · For every home

Hot panels make less power

Solar panels lose roughly 0.3 to 0.4% of output for every degree above 25°C. Spring often beats midsummer.

That is why a bright, cool April day can produce as much as a hot August one. Good airflow behind the panels helps them stay cooler.

column6: Battery cables carry the big current
column8:
☀️ Solar tip #012 · For the technical crowd

Battery cables carry the big current

A 5 kW inverter on a 48 V battery draws over 100 A. Size the cable and fuse or breaker at the battery for that.

Undersized battery leads run hot and cause voltage sag and nuisance low-voltage cut-offs. Keep them short, use proper lugs and torque them to spec.

column8:
☀️ Solar tip #013 · For every home

Expect less in winter, and plan for it

In Lebanon, a December day gives roughly half the energy of a July day: the sun is lower and the days are shorter.

Size your system and your habits for winter, not only for summer. Shift loads to midday, and keep the generator for the gaps.

Bond the frames, add surge protection

Rooftop arrays are exposed to induced surges. Keep earthing conductors short and direct, and check SPD status windows during maintenance.

Size the battery for your nights

List what must run after sunset: fridge, lights, router, TV, a fan. That list sizes your battery, not your whole bill.

Daytime loads should run directly on the panels. A battery sized for the evening and night keeps the investment reasonable and the battery working within its comfort zone.

Check the module's maximum series fuse rating and size the fuses accordingly.

Give your inverter room to breathe

Keep the inverter out of direct sun and out of closed cupboards. Heat makes it reduce its output.

Leave clearance around the unit as the manual specifies, keep the fins dust-free, and never stack boxes against it.

column6: Space rows for the winter solstice
column8:
☀️ Solar tip #018 · For the technical crowd

Space rows for the winter solstice

At Beirut's latitude the noon sun on 21 December is about 33° high. Row gap ≈ 1.55 × the rise of the panel ahead.

Rise = panel length × sin(tilt). Add a margin if you want shade-free hours beyond noon in winter.

An old fridge can cost you panels

Check the energy label. Fridges run day and night, so they matter most for your battery. Keep the door seals clean and the back coil dusted.

column8:
☀️ Solar tip #022 · For the technical crowd

Use BMS communication, not voltage guesses

Connect lithium batteries over CAN or RS485 and select the matching battery protocol. SOC becomes accurate.

Voltage-based 'user' profiles misread the flat LiFePO4 curve, leading to early cut-offs or overcharging.

Solar and the generator can be friends

Wrong charge settings are the fastest way to unbalance cells. Set absorption, float and cut-off exactly as the manufacturer specifies.

After a storm, look but don't touch

Even the switched-off panel side can carry dangerous DC voltage. If something looks wrong, switch off at the inverter and call your installer.

The right tilt for Lebanon

For a fixed system facing south, a tilt of about 25 to 30° is a good all-year compromise at Lebanon's latitude.

Steeper favours winter, flatter favours summer. Most homes are best served by the all-year compromise.

Check N–PE bonding in battery mode

When a hybrid inverter runs off-grid, the neutral–earth bond must be correct, or the RCDs downstream won't work.

The 1 kWp yardstick

Use it as a sanity check on any offer. Divide your yearly consumption by this figure to get a first idea of the system size you need.

CT clamp direction matters

A reversed CT makes the inverter think the house is exporting while it is importing. Check the live readings at commissioning.
